parts.title: Everyday Actions for a Healthier Planet
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Climate change can feel like a problem for governments and large companies, and many people ask whether their own choices make any real difference to the planet. Experts reportedly agree that politics matters most. However, daily habits can still help, especially when millions of households change together. A single action may look modest, yet it can lead to bigger changes over time. This passage looks at simple steps that ordinary people can take at home, on the road and in the shop.

Food is a good place to start, because everyone eats every day. Studies suggest that food waste may account for a large share of the emissions from our food system, so planning meals and using leftovers can help a great deal. Shoppers can write a list, buy only what is needed and freeze bread or vegetables before it goes bad. Local markets and apps that sell surplus meals can also help. Eating less meat may also help, since a plant-based diet can reportedly cut diet-related emissions by up to 49 per cent.

Energy use at home is another area where small steps add up. Switching off lights, using LED bulbs and washing clothes at a lower temperature are simple examples. According to one source, energy-efficient behaviour may cut household electricity use by up to 30 per cent, which could save families both carbon and money every year. Better insulation and a modern heating system may help even more, although they cost money at first. Repairing broken items instead of buying new ones also saves resources, and many shops now sell used goods at lower prices. It is wise not to **discard** a device when a cheap repair would make it work again.

Transport is a bigger challenge, because many people depend on cars. Flying reportedly causes about 5 per cent of global warming, so taking fewer flights is one of the strongest personal choices. For short trips, walking or cycling is cleaner, healthier and often cheaper than driving. Public buses and trains are also useful, and commuters who share rides may reduce traffic as well. Cities with safe bike lanes make it easier for residents to leave the car at home, and **those** who try cycling often enjoy it more than they expected.

Some critics argue that individual action is not enough, and they have a fair point. The idea of a personal carbon footprint was reportedly popularised by an oil company advertising campaign, which may have shifted attention away from the biggest polluters. Even so, personal choices can encourage friends, schools and workplaces to follow, and shared habits can support stronger laws. The best approach is therefore to combine daily actions with pressure on leaders and businesses. Small steps may not save the planet alone, but they are a sensible place to begin.

parts.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Promise, Tension, and the Road Ahead
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Artificial intelligence has moved from research laboratories into ordinary classrooms with remarkable speed, and tools that were once experimental have become almost **ubiquitous** in the lives of teenagers and university students. The launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 reportedly accelerated this change. Supporters see a chance to personalise learning, while critics fear new forms of dishonesty and dependence. This passage examines both views and considers how schools might respond. The debate is important because decisions made now may shape how a whole generation learns to think and work.

The idea is older than many people assume. Computer-based teaching systems such as PLATO appeared in the 1960s, and researchers later added artificial intelligence techniques to create intelligent tutoring systems that could respond to individual mistakes. Modern chatbots are more flexible, and Khanmigo reportedly offers low-cost tutoring that adapts to each learner. Language learners and students with dyslexia may also benefit from tools that explain difficult ideas patiently and repeat them as often as needed. Teachers, meanwhile, may use automation to save time on routine marking and planning.

The most visible tension concerns honesty, because a chatbot can produce a competent essay in seconds. In spring 2023, a survey reportedly found that 58 per cent of American students had used ChatGPT, and 38 per cent admitted doing so without their teacher's consent. Several school systems responded with bans, although New York City reportedly repealed its own restriction within months. Such restrictions are hard to enforce, and constant suspicion may **undermine** the trust between teachers and learners that effective teaching requires. Detection software looks like an easy answer, yet the evidence is discouraging. OpenAI reportedly withdrew its own classifier in August 2023 because of its low accuracy, and other detectors have been accused of flagging honest students by mistake. Chatbots also hallucinate, producing fluent but false information, and they can repeat biases found in their training data. Privacy is a further worry, since student writing may be stored and reused to train future models. Accuracy, bias and privacy are therefore legitimate concerns, and **these** must be weighed carefully against any educational gain.

Access is another source of unfairness, because students with fast internet and reliable modern devices can benefit far more than their classmates without them at home. Teachers also face an invisible workload, since redesigning assignments and investigating suspected misuse takes time that few schools have planned for. Training is therefore as important as technology. UNESCO guidance reportedly stresses ethical use, teacher training and data protection for schools. Policy therefore cannot be left to individual classrooms working alone. Without shared standards, enforcement may become inconsistent and leave both students and teachers guessing.

The road ahead probably lies between prohibition and uncritical enthusiasm. Schools could treat artificial intelligence as a tool to be taught, with clear rules about when it may be used, how its help should be acknowledged, and which tasks must still be completed unaided. Assessment may need to shift towards discussion, oral defence and in-class work, which are harder to outsource. Whatever approach is chosen, the aim should be to strengthen human judgement rather than replace it. If educators, parents and technology companies cooperate, artificial intelligence may become a partner in learning rather than a shortcut around it.

parts.title: The Science of Staying Healthy: Beyond Diet and Exercise
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Public advice on staying healthy usually begins and ends with what people eat and how much they move, yet the evidence suggests that this picture is incomplete. Regular physical activity is, after all, widely described as one of the most effective ways to prevent disease. However, the World Health Organization has long defined health far more broadly, as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease.

The places where people are born, grow up, live, work and age are known as the social determinants of health, and their influence is remarkably pervasive. Studies cited by public health writers reportedly suggest that more than half of a person's health is determined by these factors rather than by clinical care and genetics. A hospital can set a broken leg but cannot repair a damp flat or an unstable job.

Income is the clearest example, because researchers such as Marmot and Bell found that income and mortality are correlated in wealthy countries, with income acting as a marker of relative position in society. Education tells a similar story: adults with more schooling reportedly live longer and healthier lives than their less educated peers. Reported mortality rates among the least educated adults were roughly three times higher than among the best educated.

Work offers a striking illustration of how an apparently ordinary pattern can turn into a danger. A joint study by the World Health Organization and the International Labour Organization reportedly estimated that long working hours were linked to about 745,000 deaths from heart disease and stroke in 2016. Chronic stress and too little sleep probably contribute to such outcomes, although their exact effects are harder to measure than hours on a timesheet.

Human relationships form another dimension of health that rarely appears in conventional advice. **[1]** People are social animals, and for most of history survival depended on belonging to a group. **[2]** Older adults who live alone are reportedly much less likely to take up vaccines, and public health reviews report a strong link between social isolation and higher mortality in every age group. **[3]** That suggestion has begun to influence practice, and some health services in Britain reportedly practise social prescribing, where doctors refer patients to walking groups, choirs or volunteering projects. **[4]** Evidence for such programmes remains limited, however, and researchers continue to debate how well they work.

Recognising this, the Ottawa Charter of 1986 reportedly urged governments to treat health promotion as more than a task for hospitals and doctors. Public policy can improve housing, income and schooling, all of **which** influence health long before illness appears. Critics reasonably point out that such reforms are slow and expensive, and that individuals still bear responsibility for choices within their own control, yet the two arguments are not mutually exclusive.

Staying healthy is therefore not only a matter of discipline in the kitchen and the gym but also of the conditions that surround people's daily lives. Recognising the wider picture offers more than comfort, because it gives families, employers and governments **tangible** levers to pull. Diet and exercise remain essential, but they work best alongside secure homes, fair work and good company.

parts.title: The Endurance and Evolution of Chinese Traditional Festivals
parts.directions: Read the passage and choose the best answer (A, B, C, or D) for each question.
passage: Few cultural traditions have proved as durable as the festivals of the Chinese calendar, and about 1.5 billion people worldwide reportedly take part in Lunar New Year celebrations alone. Mainland China and Taiwan recognise four traditional festivals as statutory holidays: the Spring Festival, Qingming, the Dragon Boat Festival and the Mid-Autumn Festival. Most follow the lunar calendar, although Qingming is tied to a solar term.

Many customs are explained by legends, and the best known is the story of Nian, a beast said to attack villagers at night until red paper and loud noise drove it away. Historians trace the earliest recorded celebration to the Warring States period, in an exorcism ritual called Big Nuo, while the first mention of marking the new year comes from the Han dynasty. Red couplets, firecrackers and reunion dinners later became the visible signs of the season.

The Dragon Boat Festival, held on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, shows how **resilient** a tradition can be when its meaning is flexible. The most popular story links it to Qu Yuan, a poet and minister of Chu who drowned himself in the Miluo River, although other accounts name different figures. Some researchers suspect that the stories were later attached to older harvest and dragon-worship traditions. Even so, it became a national public holiday in 2008 and, reportedly, the first Chinese festival on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2009.

The Spring Festival remains the emotional centre of the calendar, and the wish to attend the reunion dinner drives a travel period known as chunyun, often described as the world's largest annual migration. That period reportedly begins fifteen days before New Year's Day and lasts about forty days. Gifts of money in red envelopes follow their own etiquette, since amounts containing the number eight are favoured while amounts containing four are avoided because it sounds like the word for death.

Modern life has forced some customs to change, and firecrackers, traditionally used to frighten away evil spirits, have reportedly been banned in parts of Beijing and Shanghai over several years. Hong Kong and Singapore sponsor large government fireworks displays as a substitute, so the spectacle survives even where the explosive tradition does not. Television has become a new hearth, since every mainland station reportedly broadcasts a New Year gala. Such adaptations suggest that tradition is less a fixed script than a set of adaptable meanings.

In 1928, the Kuomintang government reportedly tried to move the new year to 1 January, an attempt that was abandoned after strong opposition. **[1]** That entanglement became far more severe in 1967, when official celebrations were reportedly banned during the Cultural Revolution, although the Spring Festival had been restored as a public holiday by 1980. **[2]** Political change has therefore been as important as modernisation in shaping what people celebrate and how. **[3]** Even the name has been contested, since Yuan Shikai proposed the term Spring Festival in 1914, whereas Taiwan's government prefers Traditional Chinese New Year. **[4]** In short, festivals are never merely private occasions but also public symbols.

Today the pressure may come less from politics than from the market, as brands compete to sell gifts, food and travel packages around every major festival. Reunion dinners and dragon boat races remain central to community life, and **these** now coexist with newer, more commercial versions of each celebration. Critics fear that relentless marketing may commodify ritual, emptying it of the meaning that once defined the occasion. Yet history suggests that festivals survive because they can absorb new meanings without losing their core.

tasks.guide_md:
**1. Phân tích đề bài và xác định dạng đề:**
- Đây là dạng **Informal Email** (thư thân mật) vì người nhận là bạn bè.
- Bạn cần chia sẻ trải nghiệm cá nhân về việc sử dụng mạng xã hội bằng giọng văn tự nhiên.
- Cần trả lời đủ 3 ý chính: cách sử dụng social media, thời gian sử dụng và ảnh hưởng đến cuộc sống.
- Bài viết cần đạt tối thiểu **120 từ**, nên đưa thêm ví dụ thực tế để phát triển ý.

**2. Cách xây dựng bố cục logic (Organization):**
- **Greeting:** Mở đầu bằng lời chào thân mật. Ví dụ: Dear Lisa,
- **Opening:** Dẫn vào chủ đề. Ví dụ: Thanks for asking me about my experience with social media.
- **Body paragraph(s):** Đoạn đầu nói về cách sử dụng mạng xã hội. Đoạn sau trình bày thời gian sử dụng và tác động tích cực, tiêu cực.
- **Closing:** Kết thúc bằng suy nghĩ cá nhân. Ví dụ: I think social media is useful if we use it properly.
- **Sign-off:** Dùng cách kết thúc thân mật như Best wishes, [Your Name].

**3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Vocabulary & Grammar):**
- Sử dụng thì Hiện tại đơn để mô tả thói quen hàng ngày.
- Dùng cấu trúc both positive and negative effects để thể hiện góc nhìn cân bằng.
- Tránh chỉ nói social media is good hoặc bad, cần giải thích tác động cụ thể.
Từ vựng quan trọng:
- **Social networking sites:** Mạng xã hội
- **Online communication:** Giao tiếp trực tuyến
- **Digital platform:** Nền tảng kỹ thuật số
- **Entertainment content:** Nội dung giải trí
- **Time management:** Quản lý thời gian
- **Privacy concerns:** Lo ngại về quyền riêng tư
Từ nối (Linking words):
- **First of all:** Trước hết
- **In addition:** Ngoài ra
- **However:** Tuy nhiên
- **For example:** Ví dụ
- **As a result:** Vì vậy
Cách diễn đạt cảm xúc (Expressing feelings):
- **I find social media useful because...** Tôi thấy mạng xã hội hữu ích vì...
- **I am concerned about...** Tôi lo lắng về...
- **I believe that...** Tôi tin rằng...

**4. Các lỗi thường gặp:**
- Chỉ kể tên ứng dụng mà không giải thích cách sử dụng.
- Không đề cập thời gian sử dụng mạng xã hội.
- Chỉ nêu tác động tích cực hoặc tiêu cực mà không cân bằng.

**5. Cách kiểm tra bài trong 2 phút cuối:**
- Kiểm tra đã trả lời đủ 3 câu hỏi trong đề chưa.
- Đảm bảo email có lời chào và lời kết.
- Kiểm tra thì hiện tại, chính tả và số lượng từ.

**6. Tư duy làm bài:**
Hãy viết như đang chia sẻ thói quen thật của bản thân với bạn bè. Những ví dụ gần gũi sẽ giúp bài viết tự nhiên và dễ đạt điểm cao hơn.

GHI CHÚ CHUẨN BỊ (1 PHÚT)
GỢI Ý TRẢ LỜI
1. Phân tích đề bài:
• Đây là dạng Solution Discussion. Bạn cần chọn hoạt động tiếng Anh phù hợp nhất cho học sinh.
• Ba lựa chọn gồm talk show tiếng Anh, chương trình âm nhạc và cuộc thi tiếng Anh.
• Tiêu chí chấm điểm gồm khả năng phân tích, so sánh, lập luận và đưa ra kết luận.

2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):
• Sử dụng cấu trúc I-C-E (Introduction - Comparison/Body - End): giới thiệu mục tiêu, phân tích từng lựa chọn và kết
luận.
• Option 1 giúp học sinh luyện nghe nói và giao tiếp trong môi trường thực tế.
• Option 2 tạo không khí vui vẻ nhưng có thể tập trung nhiều vào giải trí hơn học tập.
• Option 3 tạo động lực học tập thông qua sự cạnh tranh nhưng có thể gây áp lực.
• Liên hệ với mục tiêu cải thiện tiếng Anh để chọn phương án phù hợp.
• Dùng từ nối thể hiện sự khác biệt giữa các lựa chọn.
3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):
• Không chỉ nói ưu điểm của lựa chọn mình thích mà cần đánh giá cả ba phương án.
• Dùng hiện tại đơn để mô tả hoạt động và cấu trúc so sánh để đánh giá lựa chọn.
• Nếu quên từ liên quan đến sự kiện, có thể nói về lợi ích, người tham gia và trải nghiệm.
Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:
• improve communication skills: cải thiện kỹ năng giao tiếp.
• build confidence: xây dựng sự tự tin.
• interactive activity: hoạt động tương tác.
• public speaking skills: kỹ năng nói trước đám đông.
• create a positive atmosphere: tạo không khí tích cực.
• learning experience: trải nghiệm học tập.
Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):
• Firstly: đầu tiên.
• On the other hand: mặt khác.
• Compared with: so với.
• As a result: vì vậy.
• In conclusion: kết luận.
Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:
• "I would choose Option 1 because..." - Tôi chọn phương án 1 vì...
• "The main advantage is that..." - Ưu điểm chính là...
• "Although this option is useful, it may not be the best choice because..." - Mặc dù hữu ích nhưng...
4. Các lỗi thường gặp:
• Chỉ khen phương án mình chọn mà không phân tích phương án khác.
• Lặp lại từ good hoặc interesting quá nhiều.
• Không đưa ra quyết định cuối cùng.
5. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:
• Chuyển sang các yếu tố như chi phí, số người tham gia và hiệu quả học tập.
• Dùng câu: "Let's evaluate this option from a different perspective."
• Nếu bí một ý, chuyển sang lựa chọn khác.
6. Tư duy làm bài nói:
• Suy nghĩ như người tổ chức sự kiện muốn đạt mục tiêu học tập và giải trí.
• Lựa chọn tốt cần vừa hấp dẫn vừa mang lại giá trị lâu dài.

GHI CHÚ CHUẨN BỊ (1 PHÚT)
GỢI Ý TRẢ LỜI
1. Phân tích đề bài:
• Đây là dạng Topic Development. Bạn cần phát triển chủ đề về tầm quan trọng của việc học lịch sử dựa trên các nhánh
ý và thêm ý tưởng cá nhân.
• Tiêu chí chấm điểm gồm khả năng phát triển ý, sự mạch lạc, từ vựng và ngữ pháp.
• Thời gian Part 3 là 5 phút, khoảng 3–3,5 phút cho bài nói chính và thời gian còn lại cho câu hỏi phụ.
2. Cách xây dựng bố cục khi nói (Organization):
• Sử dụng cấu trúc FEEL (Point - Explanation - Example - Link): nêu ý, giải thích, ví dụ và kết nối.
• Ví dụ 1: "Today, I would like to talk about the importance of learning history because it helps people understand the
past and learn valuable lessons."
• Ví dụ 2: "Another personal idea is that history can improve critical thinking because students need to analyze events
and their causes."
• Nhánh 4 – Ý tưởng cá nhân: Bạn có thể phát triển thêm ý về phát triển tư duy phản biện. Ví dụ: "Learning history
encourages students to think critically and understand different perspectives."
• Bám theo sơ đồ tư duy để tránh chỉ liệt kê ý mà không giải thích.
3. Chiến lược đạt điểm cao (Fluency, Vocabulary & Grammar):
• Dùng câu chuyển ý để liên kết các nhánh trong bài nói.
• Dùng Present Simple khi nói về lợi ích chung và Past Simple khi nhắc đến sự kiện lịch sử.
• Có thể thay learning history bằng studying the past hoặc historical education.
Cụm từ quan trọng nên dùng:
• historical events: sự kiện lịch sử.
• learn from the past: học hỏi từ quá khứ.
• cultural identity: bản sắc văn hóa.
• valuable lessons: bài học quý giá.
• critical thinking: tư duy phản biện.
• understand different perspectives: hiểu các góc nhìn khác nhau.
Từ nối khi nói (Linking Words):
• Firstly: đầu tiên.
• Moreover: hơn nữa.
• For example: ví dụ.
• However: tuy nhiên.
• To sum up: tóm lại.
Cách thể hiện quan điểm tự nhiên:
• "I strongly believe that..." - Tôi tin rằng...
• "From my perspective..." - Theo quan điểm của tôi...
• "It is important to remember that..." - Điều quan trọng cần nhớ là...
4. Gợi ý trả lời câu hỏi follow-up:
• "Why should young people learn history?" – Because history helps them understand their culture and avoid repeating
past mistakes.
• "Is history more important than other subjects?" – Every subject has its own value, but history helps people
understand society and human development.
• "How can teachers make history interesting?" – They can use videos, stories and real examples instead of only
teaching facts.
5. Các lỗi thường gặp:
• Chỉ kể tên lợi ích mà không giải thích.
• Quên thêm ý tưởng cá nhân ở nhánh thứ 4.
• Dành quá nhiều thời gian cho bài chính và không đủ thời gian trả lời follow-up.
6. Chiến lược xử lý khi bí ý hoặc quên từ:
• Liên hệ với kiến thức ở trường hoặc những sự kiện quen thuộc.
• Dùng câu: "That is a complex issue. If we evaluate it from a societal viewpoint..."
• Nếu quên thuật ngữ lịch sử, hãy mô tả ý bằng từ đơn giản.
7. Tư duy làm bài nói:
• Nhìn lịch sử như một công cụ giúp hiểu con người và xã hội.
• Sự logic và cách phát triển ý quan trọng hơn việc nhớ quá nhiều dữ kiện.
• Luôn đưa ví dụ thực tế để bài nói tự nhiên hơn.
